Un Bon Moment est un podcast lancé début: Un Bon Moment ("A Good Time") is a podcast launched in early 2020 by Kyan Khojandi and Navo — real name Bruno Muschio — the two writers of Bref and Bloqués. The pitch is entirely in the title: spending a good time with people you like. No theme, no segments, no common thread. They mostly host pairs of guests — Orelsan, Pierre Niney, Laurent Baffie, Thomas VDB, Morgane Cadignan, Baptiste Lecaplain — and chat for an hour and a half, sometimes two.
Le contraste avec leur passé est ce qui: The contrast with their past is what makes the show interesting. Bref was two minutes per episode, machine-gun editing, a density of shots French TV had never seen. These two are master craftsmen of compression. Here they do the exact opposite: almost no cuts, digressions within digressions. They're not people who can't do short — they're people who decided not to.
Le double de rushs pour une heure diffus: Twice the footage for one hour released, and yet almost nothing cut. After years spent compressing reality, they wanted to let it breathe.
Des gens écoutent une heure et demie de: People listen to an hour and a half of aimless conversation, right to the end, regularly. No algorithm makes that happen. That's attachment.
Chaque épisode sort en vidéo sur la chaî: Each episode comes out on video on Kyan Khojandi's channel a week before it's released as a podcast. The audio-only listener is structurally second class.
« On discute entre potes », sur le papie: "Chatting among friends" is, on paper, the pitch of ninety per cent of French podcasts — and most are unbearable. The difference comes down to one thing: these two know how to write. They craft their conversations to feel natural, which is infinitely harder than it looks. The model is also formidably efficient: two people, a few mics, light editing. Except it only works if you've spent ten years building your audience with quality writing. The cost is upfront, it's just invisible.
Deux réserves, et une demie. La première: Two and a half reservations. The first is structural: a podcast without a subject relies entirely on chemistry and the quality of the interviewer. When it clicks, it's magnificent; when it doesn't, nothing's left — and there's no way to know in advance. The second is the in-crowd feel: comedians hosting comedians, talking about the stage, tours and try-outs. Fascinating if you know that world, otherwise it's a dinner where everyone laughs at references you don't get. The half is the video released seven days before the audio: when your show is called "a good time", making part of your audience wait is a small irony.
Notre conseil d'écoute va à rebours de n: Our listening advice goes against our usual habit: don't start with a guest you don't know. Pick one you already like. This podcast doesn't sell you a topic, it sells you an evening — you might as well spend it with someone you wanted to see. In the vein of Floodcast, a little less underground.
« C'est le podcast le plus difficile à r: “It's the hardest podcast to pull off: the one with nothing to say that runs purely on chemistry. Craft disguised as idleness.”
